{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"call_2c2cc9296cb9429b98962701","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Validate tool input against the registered inputSchema\n2\t\n3\tIssue: re-cinq/HALEngine#37\n4\tLabels: priority:medium, type:feature, size:M, area:tools, epic:extension-points\n5\t\n6\tPart of #35\n7\t\n8\t## Why\n9\t\n10\t`ToolRegistry.execute` looks a tool up, logs the input's key names, and calls the executor\n11\twithout ever checking the declared `inputSchema` (`src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts`).\n12\tEvery tool declares a JSON Schema (`src/types/ai.ts`) that is handed verbatim to both\n13\tproviders, but nothing validates what comes back from the model. The shipped example shows the\n14\tshape of the problem: `example/weather-tool.ts` declares `location` as a required string, then\n15\tcasts and defaults it (`(input.location as string) || 'Unknown'`) with a comment warning the reader\n16\tthat `inputSchema` shapes what the model sends but does not enforce it. That is the careful version,\n17\twritten by the people who wrote the engine — and it still answers a malformed call with a\n18\tconfidently formatted forecast for `'Unknown'` rather than telling the model it got the call wrong.\n19\t\n20\tThe registry currently pushes this check onto each tool's own executor, leaving every consumer\n21\tto implement it itself — differently each time, or not at all. A tool that receives unexpected input must fail\n22\tin one predictable, known way before the rest of this epic's tool work can be built on top\n23\tof it.\n24\t\n25\t## What to do\n26\t\n27\tValidate `input` against the resolved tool definition's `inputSchema` inside\n28\t`ToolRegistry.execute`, before the executor runs, using a JSON Schema validator (`ajv`\n29\tunless the build proves otherwise) added to `dependencies` — not a second, hand-written\n30\tschema in a different format, since the schema already has to match what is handed to the\n31\tproviders.\n32\t\n33\tCompile a static tool's schema once at `register` time so a broken schema fails at startup,\n34\tnot mid-conversation; a schema produced by a function-valued `ToolDefinitionSource`\n35\tresolves and compiles per call, cached by the resolved schema object.\n36\t\n37\tA rejection returns a `ToolResponse` (`{result: '<what was wrong>'}`) rather than throwing,\n38\tso a malformed call becomes something the model can read and correct within the existing\n39\t`DEFAULT_MAX_TOOL_ROUNDS = 5` budget, instead of ending the whole conversation with a\n40\tgeneric transport error. Validation enforces `required`, declared types and `enum` only —\n41\tit does not inject `additionalProperties: false`, coerce types, or apply defaults, and\n42\tthere is no opt-out flag.\n43\t\n44\tUpdate `docs/adding-a-tool.md`, `README.md` and `.specify/spec.md` to match.\n45\t\n46\t## Acceptance criteria\n47\t\n48\t- [ ] `ToolRegistry.execute` validates `input` against the resolved definition's\n49\t      `inputSchema` before calling the executor; on failure it returns a `ToolResponse`\n50\t      whose `result` describes the failure, and the executor is never invoked\n51\t- [ ] A new `src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts` (the registry has no test file today)\n52\t      registers a tool requiring a `location` string, calls `execute` with `{}`, and\n53\t      asserts the returned result names `location` as required and the executor's call\n54\t      count is `0`\n55\t- [ ] A test asserts valid input with an unlisted extra property is passed through to the\n56\t      executor unchanged (`toEqual`, so an added default or coerced value fails the test) —\n57\t      exactly once\n58\t- [ ] A test asserts a wrong-typed field (a number where a string is required) is rejected\n59\t      with a message naming the field path and the expected type, and that the message does\n60\t      **not** contain the offending value\n61\t- [ ] A test asserts `register` throws at registration time for an uncompilable schema, and\n62\t      that the thrown message names the tool\n63\t- [ ] A test asserts a function-valued tool definition whose returned schema differs between\n64\t      calls is validated against the schema current at that call, not a stale cached one\n65\t- [ ] A test asserts a static tool's schema is compiled once across ten `execute` calls\n66\t- [ ] A tool-loop test in `chatOrchestrator.test.ts` drives a stub provider through a\n67\t      rejected tool call followed by a corrected retry, and asserts `processMessage`\n68\t      resolves — not rejects — with the rejection text visible to the provider on the next\n69\t      round\n70\t- [ ] `execute` still throws `Unknown tool: <name>` for an unregistered name, unchanged,\n71\t      pinned by a test\n72\t- [ ] Rejection messages and log lines name the failing property paths and the constraint\n73\t      that failed, and never a property **value**. Tool input is where identifying data\n74\t      enters the engine and the engine redacts nothing today. A test asserts a rejected\n75\t      payload containing an identifying field produces no log line and no returned text\n76\t      containing that field's value\n77\t- [ ] `execute` carries a **one-line** doc comment — `re-lint/max-comment-lines` rejects a\n78\t      `@param`/`@returns`/`@throws` block — and the full contract (rejection `ToolResponse` for input\n79\t      the schema rejects, throw only for an unknown tool name) is stated in\n80\t      `specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md`, which the comment points at\n81\t- [ ] The validator is in `package.json` `dependencies`, not `peerDependencies` or\n82\t      `devDependencies`, and\n83\t      `npm run build && node --input-type=module -e \"import('./dist/index.js')\"` exits `0`\n84\t- [ ] `README.md` states what the registry now does, and the claim is true rather than\n85\t      merely present\n86\t- [ ] `docs/adding-a-tool.md` no longer tells executors to cast defensively and handle\n87\t      missing input; it states that input reaching an executor has already passed the\n88\t      declared schema, that unknown keys may still be present, and that a rejection is\n89\t      returned to the model rather than thrown\n90\t- [ ] `.specify/spec.md` records that a rejection is a tool result (not an exception), that\n91\t      the tool-round bound is what stops a retry cycle from spinning, and that extra\n92\t      properties pass through unmodified\n93\t- [ ] The PR body states the migration note: an executor that used to hand-validate its\n94\t      input now receives only input the schema already accepts, and a tool that relied on\n95\t      seeing malformed input to produce its own error message stops seeing it. That end-to-end path is why a rejection has to be a returned\n113\t`ToolResponse` instead of a throw.\n114\t\n115\tDeliberately out of scope: the `Unknown tool: <name>` throw stays as-is — the same failure\n116\tclass handled the opposite way, which is an intentional split, but changing it affects\n117\tdirect callers and is tracked as *Return an unknown tool name to the model instead of\n118\tthrowing*. Also out of scope: validating tool *output*; hallucination detection and an\n119\tevaluation harness; per-tool authorization — a schema-valid call for someone else's data is still\n120\tvalid, and authorization is a separate `ToolContext` boundary concern that no issue in this epic\n121\towns (*Let a consumer decline a tool call through a `beforeToolCall` hook* is a veto seam, not an\n122\tauthorization model); retry, timeout\n123\tand rate limiting around tool execution; and any actual tool implementation, which is\n124\twritten against this contract later.\n125\t\n126\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"491085a4-d2ca-4f17-85a3-818e99168ec0","uuid":"1defa753-d469-4e43-b73a-425b78441137","timestamp":"2026-10-30T19:30:57.454Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"/var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/4b1232bc5957/workspace/ticket.md","content":"# Validate tool input against the registered inputSchema\n\nIssue: re-cinq/HALEngine#37\nLabels: priority:medium, type:feature, size:M, area:tools, epic:extension-points\n\nPart of #35\n\n## Why\n\n`ToolRegistry.execute` looks a tool up, logs the input's key names, and calls the executor\nwithout ever checking the declared `inputSchema` (`src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts`).\nEvery tool declares a JSON Schema (`src/types/ai.ts`) that is handed verbatim to both\nproviders, but nothing validates what comes back from the model. The shipped example shows the\nshape of the problem: `example/weather-tool.ts` declares `location` as a required string, then\ncasts and defaults it (`(input.location as string) || 'Unknown'`) with a comment warning the reader\nthat `inputSchema` shapes what the model sends but does not enforce it. That is the careful version,\nwritten by the people who wrote the engine — and it still answers a malformed call with a\nconfidently formatted forecast for `'Unknown'` rather than telling the model it got the call wrong.\n\nThe registry currently pushes this check onto each tool's own executor, leaving every consumer\nto implement it itself — differently each time, or not at all. A tool that receives unexpected input must fail\nin one predictable, known way before the rest of this epic's tool work can be built on top\nof it.\n\n## What to do\n\nValidate `input` against the resolved tool definition's `inputSchema` inside\n`ToolRegistry.execute`, before the executor runs, using a JSON Schema validator (`ajv`\nunless the build proves otherwise) added to `dependencies` — not a second, hand-written\nschema in a different format, since the schema already has to match what is handed to the\nproviders.\n\nCompile a static tool's schema once at `register` time so a broken schema fails at startup,\nnot mid-conversation; a schema produced by a function-valued `ToolDefinitionSource`\nresolves and compiles per call, cached by the resolved schema object.\n\nA rejection returns a `ToolResponse` (`{result: '<what was wrong>'}`) rather than throwing,\nso a malformed call becomes something the model can read and correct within the existing\n`DEFAULT_MAX_TOOL_ROUNDS = 5` budget, instead of ending the whole conversation with a\ngeneric transport error. Validation enforces `required`, declared types and `enum` only —\nit does not inject `additionalProperties: false`, coerce types, or apply defaults, and\nthere is no opt-out flag.\n\nUpdate `docs/adding-a-tool.md`, `README.md` and `.specify/spec.md` to match.\n\n## Acceptance criteria\n\n- [ ] `ToolRegistry.execute` validates `input` against the resolved definition's\n      `inputSchema` before calling the executor; on failure it returns a `ToolResponse`\n      whose `result` describes the failure, and the executor is never invoked\n- [ ] A new `src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts` (the registry has no test file today)\n      registers a tool requiring a `location` string, calls `execute` with `{}`, and\n      asserts the returned result names `location` as required and the executor's call\n      count is `0`\n- [ ] A test asserts valid input with an unlisted extra property is passed through to the\n      executor unchanged (`toEqual`, so an added default or coerced value fails the test) —\n      exactly once\n- [ ] A test asserts a wrong-typed field (a number where a string is required) is rejected\n      with a message naming the field path and the expected type, and that the message does\n      **not** contain the offending value\n- [ ] A test asserts `register` throws at registration time for an uncompilable schema, and\n      that the thrown message names the tool\n- [ ] A test asserts a function-valued tool definition whose returned schema differs between\n      calls is validated against the schema current at that call, not a stale cached one\n- [ ] A test asserts a static tool's schema is compiled once across ten `execute` calls\n- [ ] A tool-loop test in `chatOrchestrator.test.ts` drives a stub provider through a\n      rejected tool call followed by a corrected retry, and asserts `processMessage`\n      resolves — not rejects — with the rejection text visible to the provider on the next\n      round\n- [ ] `execute` still throws `Unknown tool: <name>` for an unregistered name, unchanged,\n      pinned by a test\n- [ ] Rejection messages and log lines name the failing property paths and the constraint\n      that failed, and never a property **value**. Tool input is where identifying data\n      enters the engine and the engine redacts nothing today. A test asserts a rejected\n      payload containing an identifying field produces no log line and no returned text\n      containing that field's value\n- [ ] `execute` carries a **one-line** doc comment — `re-lint/max-comment-lines` rejects a\n      `@param`/`@returns`/`@throws` block — and the full contract (rejection `ToolResponse` for input\n      the schema rejects, throw only for an unknown tool name) is stated in\n      `specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md`, which the comment points at\n- [ ] The validator is in `package.json` `dependencies`, not `peerDependencies` or\n      `devDependencies`, and\n      `npm run build && node --input-type=module -e \"import('./dist/index.js')\"` exits `0`\n- [ ] `README.md` states what the registry now does, and the claim is true rather than\n      merely present\n- [ ] `docs/adding-a-tool.md` no longer tells executors to cast defensively and handle\n      missing input; it states that input reaching an executor has already passed the\n      declared schema, that unknown keys may still be present, and that a rejection is\n      returned to the model rather than thrown\n- [ ] `.specify/spec.md` records that a rejection is a tool result (not an exception), that\n      the tool-round bound is what stops a retry cycle from spinning, and that extra\n      properties pass through unmodified\n- [ ] The PR body states the migration note: an executor that used to hand-validate its\n      input now receives only input the schema already accepts, and a tool that relied on\n      seeing malformed input to produce its own error message stops seeing it. The version\n      bump is MINOR\n- [ ] Every test this issue adds cites the statement it validates with an inline\n      `([validated by ...])` link in a `specs/**` or `adrs/**` file, and the statements exist\n      before the tests do. `re-lint/require-spec-link` fails the build on an uncited test, so the\n      spec edits are part of this issue rather than a follow-up\n- [ ] `CHANGELOG.md` carries an entry for this change, written for somebody reading it on npm\n      rather than somebody reading this repo's log. CI runs `scripts/check-changelog.sh` and\n      fails any PR touching a non-test file under `src/` without one\n- [ ] `npm run build`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm test`, `npm run eslint` (`--max-warnings 0`)\n      and `npm run prettier:check` pass, with no `any` in the changed public surface\n\n## Tech notes\n\nToday's `throw` in `registry.ts` propagates through the orchestrator's tool-call\n`Promise.all`, out of the processing loop's `try`, fires `onError`, and reaches the\nWebSocket error handler, which sends a generic \"Failed to process message\" and never sends\nthe stream-end frame. That end-to-end path is why a rejection has to be a returned\n`ToolResponse` instead of a throw.\n\nDeliberately out of scope: the `Unknown tool: <name>` throw stays as-is — the same failure\nclass handled the opposite way, which is an intentional split, but changing it affects\ndirect callers and is tracked as *Return an unknown tool name to the model instead of\nthrowing*. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"call_46cd3444531a4e4088cb0b21","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Tool Responses\n2\t\n3\t| Field  | Value |\n4\t| ------ | ----- |\n5\t| Issue  | n/a   |\n6\t| Status | Draft |\n7\t\n8\tBy default, a tool executor returns a plain string that feeds back into the AI conversation. The client never sees the result -- it only sees the tool invocation (name and input parameters). This is fine for most tools, but sometimes a tool knows exactly what to show the user and does not need the AI to rephrase it.\n9\t\n10\tThe `ToolResponse` interface gives tools two additional capabilities:\n11\t\n12\t1. **Client messages** -- send one or more WebSocket messages directly to the client\n13\t2. **Suppress the AI response** -- keep the model's reply in conversation context but hide it from the client\n14\t\n15\tThese are opt-in. Tools that return a plain string continue to work exactly as before.\n16\t\n17\t## The ToolResponse Interface\n18\t\n19\t<!-- doc-block: src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts#ToolResponse -->\n20\t```typescript\n21\tinterface ToolResponse {\n22\t  result: string;\n23\t  clientMessages?: OutgoingMessage[];\n24\t  suppressAssistantResponse?: boolean;\n25\t}\n26\t```\n27\t\n28\t| Field | Purpose |\n29\t|-------|---------|\n30\t| `result` | The string the AI model sees -- identical to what a plain-string executor returns |\n31\t| `clientMessages` | Optional array of `OutgoingMessage` values sent directly to the client via WebSocket |\n32\t| `suppressAssistantResponse` | When `true`, the AI's next text response still accumulates in `session.entries` for context continuity, but is not sent to the client |\n33\t\n34\tA `ToolExecutor` can return either a plain `string` or a `ToolResponse`:\n35\t\n36\t<!-- doc-block: src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts#ToolExecutor -->\n37\t```typescript\n38\ttype ToolExecutor = (input: Record<string, unknown>, context?: ToolContext) => Promise<string | ToolResponse>;\n39\t```\n40\t\n41\t`context` carries the session the call belongs to -- `userId`, `sessionId`, `workspaceId`, and the `authHeaders` forwarded from the WebSocket upgrade, so a tool can proxy the caller's credentials upstream.\n42\t\n43\tThe registry normalizes both forms internally via `normalizeToolResponse()`, so downstream code always sees a `ToolResponse`.\n44\t\n45\t## When to Use This\n46\t\n47\t**Client messages** make sense when the tool result is self-explanatory and the AI does not need to interpret it for the user. A unit conversion, a status update, a formatted data table -- these are cases where the tool knows the best presentation and the AI would just parrot the same information.\n48\t\n49\t**Suppression** pairs naturally with client messages. If the tool already sent the answer to the client, the AI's follow-up (\"The conversion result is 160.93 km\") adds no value. Suppression hides that echo while keeping it in the conversation so the AI remembers the context for follow-up questions.\n50\t\n51\tUse plain string returns (the default) when the AI needs to interpret or summarize the tool result for the user. Database lookups and search results are good examples -- the raw data benefits from the AI explaining it in context.\n52\t\n53\t## Data Flow\n54\t\n55\t```\n56\tPlain string:    executor returns \"data\"\n57\t                   -> normalizeToolResponse wraps to {result: \"data\"}\n58\t                   -> orchestrator feeds result to AI\n59\t                   -> AI responds, client sees the response\n60\t\n61\tWith client messages:\n62\t                 executor returns {result, clientMessages, suppressAssistantResponse}\n63\t                   -> orchestrator extracts .result for AI (unchanged)\n64\t                   -> orchestrator yields tool_result chunk carrying clientMessages\n65\t                   -> if suppress, orchestrator yields suppress_output chunk\n66\t                   -> messageHandler sends clientMessages to client\n67\t                   -> messageHandler blanks pre-tool assistant entries (entry_upsert with empty content)\n68\t                   -> messageHandler skips WebSocket sends for suppressed entries\n69\t                   -> messageHandler sends entry_skip for each new suppressed entry\n70\t                   -> suppressed entries still accumulate in session.entries\n71\t                   -> client adjusts incoming indices using tracked skip list\n72\t```\n73\t\n74\tThe key insight: suppressed entries are invisible to the client but visible to the AI. The conversation context stays intact, so the model can reference previous tool results even when the user did not see the AI's commentary on them.\n75\t\n76\t## Example: Unit Converter\n77\t\n78\tThe `convert_units` tool demonstrates all three features: client messages, suppression, and index assignment. A conversion like \"100 miles to kilometers\" has a definitive answer -- the AI does not need to elaborate.\n79\t\n80\t<!-- doc-block: none -- a simplified tool, marked simplified in its own first line -->\n81\t```typescript\n82\t// src/orchestration/tools/unitConverterTool.ts (simplified)\n83\t\n84\texport const executeUnitConverter: ToolExecutor = async (input) => {\n85\t  const value = input.value as number;\n86\t  const fromUnit = (input.from_unit as string) || '';\n87\t  const toUnit = (input.to_unit as string) || '';\n88\t\n89\t  const result = convert(value, fromUnit, toUnit);\n90\t\n91\t  if (!result) {\n92\t    // Error case: return plain string so AI can explain the problem\n93\t    return JSON.stringify({error: `Cannot convert from \"${fromUnit}\" to \"${toUnit}\".`});\n94\t  }\n95\t\n96\t  return {\n97\t    result: JSON.stringify({value, fromUnit, toUnit, converted: result.converted, formatted: result.formatted}),\n98\t    clientMessages: [\n99\t      {\n100\t        type: 'entry_upsert',\n101\t        index: 0,\n102\t        entry: {role: 'assistant', content: result.formatted, timestamp: new Date().toISOString(), isStreaming: false},\n103\t      },\n104\t    ],\n105\t    suppressAssistantResponse: true,\n106\t  };\n107\t};\n108\t```\n109\t\n110\tNotice three things:\n111\t\n112\t1. On success, the executor returns a `clientMessages` array with an `entry_upsert` containing the formatted result. The client receives this as an assistant entry. The `index` is set to `0` -- the orchestrator replaces it with the correct session index (see \"Index assignment\" below).\n113\t\n114\t2. `suppressAssistantResponse: true` hides the AI's follow-up. The AI still receives the result string (so it has context for follow-ups), but the client does not see the AI echoing \"100 miles equals 160.93 km.\"\n115\t\n116\t3. On error, the executor returns a plain string. This lets the AI explain what went wrong in its own words -- \"I could not convert miles to knots because they measure different things.\"\n117\t\n118\t## Adding Client Messages\n119\t\n120\tIf the tool wants to send a custom message to the client, use `clientMessages`. Any valid `OutgoingMessage` type works -- `entry_upsert`, `entry_delta`, `entry_commit`, or `error`.\n121\t\n122\t<!-- doc-block: none -- a worked executor showing one return shape, not code this package exports -->\n123\t```typescript\n124\texport const executeMyTool: ToolExecutor = async (input) => {\n125\t  const data = await fetchSomething(input);\n126\t\n127\t  return {\n128\t    result: JSON.stringify(data),\n129\t    clientMessages: [\n130\t      {type: 'entry_upsert', index: 0, entry: {\n131\t        role: 'assistant' as const,\n132\t        content: formatData(data),\n133\t        timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),\n134\t        isStreaming: false,\n135\t      }},\n136\t    ],\n137\t  };\n138\t};\n139\t```\n140\t\n141\tClient messages are forwarded to the WebSocket after index assignment. The client processes them through its existing message dispatch pipeline -- no client-side changes needed.\n142\t\n143\t### Index assignment for entry_upsert\n144\t\n145\tTools do not have access to the session, so they cannot know the correct entry index. The orchestrator handles this automatically: any `entry_upsert` message in `clientMessages` gets its `index` replaced with the real value by appending the entry to the session. The tool can set `index` to any value -- it will be overwritten.\n146\t\n147\tThis means the entry also becomes part of the session's `entries` array, maintaining context continuity for the AI model.\n148\t\n149\t## How It Works Under the Hood\n150\t\n151\t### Orchestrator\n152\t\n153\tAfter executing tool calls, `chatOrchestrator.ts` checks each `ToolResponse` for client messages and suppression flags:\n154\t\n155\t<!-- doc-block: none -- the orchestrator fragment that normalises responses, quoted out of its function -->\n156\t```typescript\n157\tconst responses = await Promise.all(\n158\t  pendingToolCalls.map(async (tc) => {\n159\t    const response = await toolRegistry.execute(tc.name, tc.input);\n160\t    return {tc, response};\n161\t  })\n162\t);\n163\t\n164\t// Collect client messages from all tools\n165\tconst clientMessages = responses.flatMap(({response}) => response.clientMessages ?? []);\n166\t\n167\t// Yield them as a chunk for the message handler\n168\tif (clientMessages.length > 0) {\n169\t  yield {type: 'tool_result', clientMessages};\n170\t}\n171\t\n172\t// Signal suppression if any tool requested it\n173\tif (responses.some(({response}) => response.suppressAssistantResponse)) {\n174\t  yield {type: 'suppress_output'};\n175\t}\n176\t```\n177\t\n178\t### Message Handler\n179\t\n180\tTwo new chunk types flow through `processChunk`:\n181\t\n182\t- `tool_result` -- each client message in the array is serialized and sent directly to the WebSocket\n183\t- `suppress_output` -- sets `state.suppressOutput = true` on the stream state\n184\t\n185\tWhen suppression is active, `streamSegment` and `commitAndClear` still call `appendEntry`, `appendDelta`, and `commitEntry` (so the session accumulates entries for context), but skip `sendUpsert`, `sendDelta`, and `sendCommit` (so the client sees nothing).\n186\t\n187\tWhen a new entry is created under suppression, the server sends an `entry_skip` message with the server-side index. This tells the client \"an entry exists here on the server, but you will never receive it.\" The client tracks these skipped indices and adjusts all subsequent incoming indices via the `adjustIndex` pure function. Without this, server indices would diverge from the client's entry array, causing deltas and commits to target the wrong positions.\n188\t\n189\tIf the AI streamed text *before* the tool call (which happens when the model explains what it is about to do), that text was already sent to the client as an assistant entry. When suppression activates, the server retroactively blanks these entries by sending `entry_upsert` with empty content. The client already skips rendering empty assistant entries, so the pre-tool text disappears cleanly.\n190\t\n191\t**Suppression is sticky for the entire stream.** Once a tool sets `suppressAssistantResponse: true` in any round, all subsequent AI responses in that stream are suppressed -- even if later tool rounds do not set the flag. This is intentional: suppression is a per-message property, not per-round. If the first tool already sent the definitive answer to the client, the AI's commentary in all following rounds is equally redundant. A new user message starts a fresh stream with `suppressOutput: false`.\n192\t\n193\t### stream_end and the spinner\n194\t\n195\tThe server sends a `stream_end` message after every completed stream (see [websocket-protocol.md](../hal-engine-websocket-protocol/spec.md)). This is the client's signal to clear loading indicators.\n196\t\n197\tWithout `stream_end`, suppression would cause the tool spinner to hang forever. When the assistant response is suppressed, no `entry_upsert` arrives after the tool entry, so the tool stays as the last entry in the array. The client tracks an `isProcessing` state: `true` when the user sends a message, `false` when `stream_end` arrives. The spinner only shows when the tool is both last in the list *and* the stream is still processing.\n198\t\n199\t### MessageChunk union\n200\t\n201\tThe `MessageChunk` type gained two variants:\n202\t\n203\t<!-- doc-block: src/types/ai.ts#MessageChunk -->\n204\t```typescript\n205\ttype MessageChunk =\n206\t  | {type: 'text'; text: string}\n207\t```\n208\t\n209\tThese two variants are internal plumbing -- they never leave the server. The client only sees standard `OutgoingMessage` types over the WebSocket.\n210\t\n211\t## File Reference\n212\t\n213\t| File | What changed |\n214\t|------|-------------|\n215\t| `src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts` | `ToolResponse` interface, widened `ToolExecutor`, `normalizeToolResponse()` |\n216\t| `src/types/ai.ts` | `tool_result` and `suppress_output` variants on `MessageChunk` |\n217\t| `src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.ts` | `executeToolCalls` returns `ToolExecutionResult`, yields new chunks |\n218\t| `src/transport/ws/messageHandler.ts` | `suppressOutput` on stream state, `processToolResultChunk`, guarded sends, `entry_skip`, blanking |\n219\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"491085a4-d2ca-4f17-85a3-818e99168ec0","uuid":"56244d0e-ca79-4204-a675-3920e98a77da","timestamp":"2026-10-30T19:31:21.277Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"/var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/4b1232bc5957/workspace/target/specs/hal-engine-tool-responses/spec.md","content":"# Tool Responses\n\n| Field  | Value |\n| ------ | ----- |\n| Issue  | n/a   |\n| Status | Draft |\n\nBy default, a tool executor returns a plain string that feeds back into the AI conversation. The client never sees the result -- it only sees the tool invocation (name and input parameters). This is fine for most tools, but sometimes a tool knows exactly what to show the user and does not need the AI to rephrase it.\n\nThe `ToolResponse` interface gives tools two additional capabilities:\n\n1. **Client messages** -- send one or more WebSocket messages directly to the client\n2. **Suppress the AI response** -- keep the model's reply in conversation context but hide it from the client\n\nThese are opt-in. Tools that return a plain string continue to work exactly as before.\n\n## The ToolResponse Interface\n\n<!-- doc-block: src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts#ToolResponse -->\n```typescript\ninterface ToolResponse {\n  result: string;\n  clientMessages?: OutgoingMessage[];\n  suppressAssistantResponse?: boolean;\n}\n```\n\n| Field | Purpose |\n|-------|---------|\n| `result` | The string the AI model sees -- identical to what a plain-string executor returns |\n| `clientMessages` | Optional array of `OutgoingMessage` values sent directly to the client via WebSocket |\n| `suppressAssistantResponse` | When `true`, the AI's next text response still accumulates in `session.entries` for context continuity, but is not sent to the client |\n\nA `ToolExecutor` can return either a plain `string` or a `ToolResponse`:\n\n<!-- doc-block: src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts#ToolExecutor -->\n```typescript\ntype ToolExecutor = (input: Record<string, unknown>, context?: ToolContext) => Promise<string | ToolResponse>;\n```\n\n`context` carries the session the call belongs to -- `userId`, `sessionId`, `workspaceId`, and the `authHeaders` forwarded from the WebSocket upgrade, so a tool can proxy the caller's credentials upstream.\n\nThe registry normalizes both forms internally via `normalizeToolResponse()`, so downstream code always sees a `ToolResponse`.\n\n## When to Use This\n\n**Client messages** make sense when the tool result is self-explanatory and the AI does not need to interpret it for the user. A unit conversion, a status update, a formatted data table -- these are cases where the tool knows the best presentation and the AI would just parrot the same information.\n\n**Suppression** pairs naturally with client messages. If the tool already sent the answer to the client, the AI's follow-up (\"The conversion result is 160.93 km\") adds no value. Suppression hides that echo while keeping it in the conversation so the AI remembers the context for follow-up questions.\n\nUse plain string returns (the default) when the AI needs to interpret or summarize the tool result for the user. Database lookups and search results are good examples -- the raw data benefits from the AI explaining it in context.\n\n## Data Flow\n\n```\nPlain string:    executor returns \"data\"\n                   -> normalizeToolResponse wraps to {result: \"data\"}\n                   -> orchestrator feeds result to AI\n                   -> AI responds, client sees the response\n\nWith client messages:\n                 executor returns {result, clientMessages, suppressAssistantResponse}\n                   -> orchestrator extracts .result for AI (unchanged)\n                   -> orchestrator yields tool_result chunk carrying clientMessages\n                   -> if suppress, orchestrator yields suppress_output chunk\n                   -> messageHandler sends clientMessages to client\n                   -> messageHandler blanks pre-tool assistant entries (entry_upsert with empty content)\n                   -> messageHandler skips WebSocket sends for suppressed entries\n                   -> messageHandler sends entry_skip for each new suppressed entry\n                   -> suppressed entries still accumulate in session.entries\n                   -> client adjusts incoming indices using tracked skip list\n```\n\nThe key insight: suppressed entries are invisible to the client but visible to the AI. The conversation context stays intact, so the model can reference previous tool results even when the user did not see the AI's commentary on them.\n\n## Example: Unit Converter\n\nThe `convert_units` tool demonstrates all three features: client messages, suppression, and index assignment. A conversion like \"100 miles to kilometers\" has a definitive answer -- the AI does not need to elaborate.\n\n<!-- doc-block: none -- a simplified tool, marked simplified in its own first line -->\n```typescript\n// src/orchestration/tools/unitConverterTool.ts (simplified)\n\nexport const executeUnitConverter: ToolExecutor = async (input) => {\n  const value = input.value as number;\n  const fromUnit = (input.from_unit as string) || '';\n  const toUnit = (input.to_unit as string) || '';\n\n  const result = convert(value, fromUnit, toUnit);\n\n  if (!result) {\n    // Error case: return plain string so AI can explain the problem\n    return JSON.stringify({error: `Cannot convert from \"${fromUnit}\" to \"${toUnit}\".`});\n  }\n\n  return {\n    result: JSON.stringify({value, fromUnit, toUnit, converted: result.converted, formatted: result.formatted}),\n    clientMessages: [\n      {\n        type: 'entry_upsert',\n        index: 0,\n        entry: {role: 'assistant', content: result.formatted, timestamp: new Date().toISOString(), isStreaming: false},\n      },\n    ],\n    suppressAssistantResponse: true,\n  };\n};\n```\n\nNotice three things:\n\n1. On success, the executor returns a `clientMessages` array with an `entry_upsert` containing the formatted result. The client receives this as an assistant entry. The `index` is set to `0` -- the orchestrator replaces it with the correct session index (see \"Index assignment\" below).\n\n2. `suppressAssistantResponse: true` hides the AI's follow-up. The AI still receives the result string (so it has context for follow-ups), but the client does not see the AI echoing \"100 miles equals 160.93 km.\"\n\n3. On error, the executor returns a plain string. This lets the AI explain what went wrong in its own words -- \"I could not convert miles to knots because they measure different things.\"\n\n## Adding Client Messages\n\nIf the tool wants to send a custom message to the client, use `clientMessages`. Any valid `OutgoingMessage` type works -- `entry_upsert`, `entry_delta`, `entry_commit`, or `error`.\n\n<!-- doc-block: none -- a worked executor showing one return shape, not code this package exports -->\n```typescript\nexport const executeMyTool: ToolExecutor = async (input) => {\n  const data = await fetchSomething(input);\n\n  return {\n    result: JSON.stringify(data),\n    clientMessages: [\n      {type: 'entry_upsert', index: 0, entry: {\n        role: 'assistant' as const,\n        content: formatData(data),\n        timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),\n        isStreaming: false,\n      }},\n    ],\n  };\n};\n```\n\nClient messages are forwarded to the WebSocket after index assignment. The client processes them through its existing message dispatch pipeline -- no client-side changes needed.\n\n### Index assignment for entry_upsert\n\nTools do not have access to the session, so they cannot know the correct entry index. The orchestrator handles this automatically: any `entry_upsert` message in `clientMessages` gets its `index` replaced with the real value by appending the entry to the session. The tool can set `index` to any value -- it will be overwritten.\n\nThis means the entry also becomes part of the session's `entries` array, maintaining context continuity for the AI model.\n\n## How It Works Under the Hood\n\n### Orchestrator\n\nAfter executing tool calls, `chatOrchestrator.ts` checks each `ToolResponse` for client messages and suppression flags:\n\n<!-- doc-block: none -- the orchestrator fragment that normalises responses, quoted out of its function -->\n```typescript\nconst responses = await Promise.all(\n  pendingToolCalls.map(async (tc) => {\n    const response = await toolRegistry.execute(tc.name, tc.input);\n    return {tc, response};\n  })\n);\n\n// Collect client messages from all tools\nconst clientMessages = responses.flatMap(({response}) => response.clientMessages ?? []);\n\n// Yield them as a chunk for the message handler\nif (clientMessages.length > 0) {\n  yield {type: 'tool_result', clientMessages};\n}\n\n// Signal suppression if any tool requested it\nif (responses.some(({response}) => response.suppressAssistantResponse)) {\n  yield {type: 'suppress_output'};\n}\n```\n\n### Message Handler\n\nTwo new chunk types flow through `processChunk`:\n\n- `tool_result` -- each client message in the array is serialized and sent directly to the WebSocket\n- `suppress_output` -- sets `state.suppressOutput = true` on the stream state\n\nWhen suppression is active, `streamSegment` and `commitAndClear` still call `appendEntry`, `appendDelta`, and `commitEntry` (so the session accumulates entries for context), but skip `sendUpsert`, `sendDelta`, and `sendCommit` (so the client sees nothing).\n\nWhen a new entry is created under suppression, the server sends an `entry_skip` message with the server-side index. This tells the client \"an entry exists here on the server, but you will never receive it.\" The client tracks these skipped indices and adjusts all subsequent incoming indices via the `adjustIndex` pure function. When suppression activates, the server retroactively blanks these entries by sending `entry_upsert` with empty content. This is intentional: suppression is a per-message property, not per-round. If the first tool already sent the definitive answer to the client, the AI's commentary in all following rounds is equally redundant. A new user message starts a fresh stream with `suppressOutput: false`.\n\n### stream_end and the spinner\n\nThe server sends a `stream_end` message after every completed stream (see [websocket-protocol.md](../hal-engine-websocket-protocol/spec.md)). This is the client's signal to clear loading indicators.\n\nWithout `stream_end`, suppression would cause the tool spinner to hang forever. When the assistant response is suppressed, no `entry_upsert` arrives after the tool entry, so the tool stays as the last entry in the array. The client tracks an `isProcessing` state: `true` when the user sends a message, `false` when `stream_end` arrives. The client only sees standard `OutgoingMessage` types over the WebSocket.\n\n## File Reference\n\n| File | What changed |\n|------|-------------|\n| `src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts` | `ToolResponse` interface, widened `ToolExecutor`, `normalizeToolResponse()` |\n| `src/types/ai.ts` | `tool_result` and `suppress_output` variants on `MessageChunk` |\n| `src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.ts` | `executeToolCalls` returns `ToolExecutionResult`, yields new chunks |\n| `src/transport/ws/messageHandler.ts` | `suppressOutput` on stream state, `processToolResultChunk`, guarded sends, `entry_skip`, blanking |\n","numLines":219,"startLine":1,"totalLines":219}},"tool_result_meta":[{"id":"call_46cd3444531a4e4088cb0b21","permission_decision":{"decision":"accept","source":"config","reason_type":"mode"}}]}

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"call_19706c38502549fdbc0d1bdd","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Lore test-command interface (lore_list_tests / lore_run_test).\n2\t# Written for this repo's Jest suite rather than adapted from the Vitest\n3\t# equivalent for a Vitest suite: the report shapes happen to match, but the\n4\t# invocations do not.\n5\t- id: hal-engine-jest\n6\t  name: HAL Engine Jest suite\n7\t  cwd: .\n8\t  description: >-\n9\t    The ts-jest unit suite over src/ and scripts/ (jest.config.js roots), run\n10\t    on every pull request in .github/workflows/ci.yml as the \"Test\" step.\n11\t    Selectors are \"<repo-relative-file>::<full test name>\" as emitted by the\n12\t    list command. Jest has no dry-run, so the list command executes the suite\n13\t    once with --json and derives every name from the report; it deliberately\n14\t    tolerates a red suite, since listing must not depend on the tests passing.\n15\t    The run command selects one test with --runTestsByPath plus an anchored,\n16\t    regex-escaped -t, and treats a selector that matches nothing as a failure\n17\t    rather than a green run of an empty suite. Neither command builds first:\n18\t    no test here reads dist/.\n19\t  list: node scripts/lore-list-tests.mjs\n20\t  run: node scripts/lore-run-test.mjs \"{selector}\"\n21\t  coverage_format: lcov\n22\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"491085a4-d2ca-4f17-85a3-818e99168ec0","uuid":"d8ed98ba-2552-47d3-a64c-2616416c4096","timestamp":"2026-10-30T19:31:37.788Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"/var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/4b1232bc5957/workspace/target/.lore/test-commands.yml","content":"# Lore test-command interface (lore_list_tests / lore_run_test).\n# Written for this repo's Jest suite rather than adapted from the Vitest\n# equivalent for a Vitest suite: the report shapes happen to match, but the\n# invocations do not.\n- id: hal-engine-jest\n  name: HAL Engine Jest suite\n  cwd: .\n  description: >-\n    The ts-jest unit suite over src/ and scripts/ (jest.config.js roots), run\n    on every pull request in .github/workflows/ci.yml as the \"Test\" step.\n    Selectors are \"<repo-relative-file>::<full test name>\" as emitted by the\n    list command. Jest has no dry-run, so the list command executes the suite\n    once with --json and derives every name from the report; it deliberately\n    tolerates a red suite, since listing must not depend on the tests passing.\n    The run command selects one test with --runTestsByPath plus an anchored,\n    regex-escaped -t, and treats a selector that matches nothing as a failure\n    rather than a green run of an empty suite. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"call_468b45cf53d84eecb235f2b6","type":"tool_result","content":"66:## Spec Header Table\n67-\n68-Every `specs/*/spec.md` opens with its title, then a two-column header table,\n69-and carries a lead paragraph of prose before its first `##` section:\n70-\n71-```markdown\n72-# <spec title>\n73-\n74-| Field  | Value                  |\n75-| ------ | ---------------------- |\n76-| Issue  | re-cinq/HALEngine#<n> |\n77-| Status | Draft                  |\n78-\n79-<lead paragraph>\n80-```\n81-\n82-The lead paragraph does not have to sit immediately after the table: a spec\n83-carrying a metadata block of its own may place that block between the two. What\n84-the convention requires is that prose, rather than a section heading, follows\n85-the header material, and that the prose runs to at least 40 characters -\n86-anything shorter is reported as no lead paragraph at all.\n87-\n88-`Issue` names the issue the spec was written against, or `n/a` for the specs\n89-that predate this convention.\n90-\n91-`Status` is one of `Draft`, `In Progress` or `Shipped`. It is not a mood, and\n92-it is not a claim about how finished the feature is: it is the spec's own\n93-test-citation coverage. No testable statement cited is `Draft`, some cited is\n94-`In Progress`, all cited is `Shipped`. A spec describing shipped, working\n95-behaviour still reads `Draft` until its statements cite the tests that\n96-validate them.\n97-\n98-A spec that should no longer be graded takes a terminal value instead. The\n99-parser buckets roughly sixteen labels into five buckets, and the two terminal\n100-ones skip the coverage check whatever the citation count:\n101-\n102-| Written into the spec                                            | Bucket                       |\n103-| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |\n104-| `Draft`                                                          | `draft`                      |\n105-| `In Progress`, `In Review`, `Planning`, `WIP`, `Proposed`        | `in-progress`                |\n106-| `Shipped`, `Implemented`, `Complete`, `Accepted`, `Done`, `Live` | `shipped`                    |\n107-| `Retired`, `Superseded`, `Removed`, `Deprecated`, `Obsolete`     | `retired` - skips the check  |\n108-| `Rejected`, `Abandoned`                                          | `rejected` - skips the check |\n109-\n110-Prefer the canonical `Draft` / `In Progress` / `Shipped` for a live spec; reach\n111-for `Retired` or `Rejected` rather than leaving a superseded spec to claim a\n112-coverage tier it will never earn.\n113-\n114-ADRs do not carry this table. They declare their state as YAML frontmatter\n115-`status:` instead - `accepted` for a decision the code implements, `proposed`\n116-for one it does not. That field does mean maturity, which the spec `Status` row\n117-explicitly does not. The difference is deliberate: ADRs are exempt from the\n118-coverage tier, because asking a decision record to cite a test for every\n119-statement it makes is the wrong ask of a decision record.\n120-\n121-`.specify/spec.md` is exempt from this section. It is the repo-level system\n122-spec, it predates the convention, and its content is deliberately frozen -\n123-giving it a header table and a lead paragraph would mean writing new prose into\n124-a file that is meant to stay unchanged. The exemption covers the header table\n125-and the lead paragraph only: the Lore coverage job does scan\n126-`.specify/spec.md`, so link placement still applies to it.","is_error":false}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"491085a4-d2ca-4f17-85a3-818e99168ec0","uuid":"ea92beba-0189-4661-95b4-9e3f846844fd","timestamp":"2026-10-30T19:31:42.347Z","tool_use_result":{"stdout":"66:## Spec Header Table\n67-\n68-Every `specs/*/spec.md` opens with its title, then a two-column header table,\n69-and carries a lead paragraph of prose before its first `##` section:\n70-\n71-```markdown\n72-# <spec title>\n73-\n74-| Field  | Value                  |\n75-| ------ | ---------------------- |\n76-| Issue  | re-cinq/HALEngine#<n> |\n77-| Status | Draft                  |\n78-\n79-<lead paragraph>\n80-```\n81-\n82-The lead paragraph does not have to sit immediately after the table: a spec\n83-carrying a metadata block of its own may place that block between the two. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"call_3b7b9eadc53d489b83d12bc7","type":"tool_result","content":"128:## Spec Test Links\n129-\n130-Statements in `specs/*/spec.md` cite their validating test in a trailing\n131-parenthetical at the end of the statement, where a list item counts as one\n132-statement and a paragraph counts per sentence. Tests live beside their source\n133-in this repo, so the path points into `src/`:\n134-\n135-```markdown\n136-- All entries within a single assistant response are committed before the next\n137-  user message is processed\n138-  ([validated by: commits every entry before the next user message](../../src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.test.ts#L42)).\n139-```\n140-\n141-The citation carries the test's **name** as well as its line. The name is what the\n142-author cited; the line is a derived pointer, and it goes stale on its own - adding\n143-an import above a suite moves every test below it, and the citation lands on a\n144-different, still-valid declaration without anything noticing. `npm run spec:names`\n145-holds each citation to the test it names, and `npm run spec:names:fix` repoints the\n146-line from the name. The `#Lnn` stays because the lint rule and the coverage job\n147-both index by it; a citation without one marks the whole file covered rather than\n148-one test.\n149-\n150-A citation counts as coverage only where it is trailing, and a test link placed\n151-anywhere else in the statement is a misplaced citation rather than a weaker one.\n152-Upstream `check:spec-links` reports it and exits 1, and the coverage job that\n153-consumes these specs records nothing for it - so a spec can read as fully cited while its coverage is\n154-zero. A mid-statement link to something that is not a test file - a script, a\n155-doc, another spec - is ordinary prose, is never reported, and was never coverage\n156-to begin with. A misplaced citation is fixed by moving it to the end of its\n157-statement, never by deleting it.\n158-\n159-In a test file the `#Lnn` anchor must land on the `it(`, `test(` or `describe(`\n160-declaration itself - not a blank line, not one holding only closing punctuation,\n161-and not a line inside the test body. A citation onto an `expect` renders and\n162-resolves like any other, and proves nothing: no reader can turn that line back\n163-into the name of a case. `scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.mjs` reports all four as\n164-`rotten` and exits 1 in both modes. A citation into a file that is not a test -\n165-a workflow, a config, `package.json` - has no declaration to land on and is held\n166-only to existing and carrying content.\n167-\n168-What no gate can catch is an anchor aimed at the wrong declaration: a real but\n169-unintended `it(` passes every check. The tell is that the test the statement\n170-meant to cite goes on reading as uncited in the `require-spec-link` backlog.\n171-\n172-Anchors drift silently whenever a cited file gains or loses lines above them, so\n173-after editing any cited file re-run `node scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.mjs`\n174-rather than hand-correcting the numbers. That script cannot repair a spec absent\n175-from the base ref, since it has no baseline to translate from; on the branch that\n176-introduces a spec, its anchors have to be corrected by hand.\n177-\n178-The convention's tooling is wired up here: `npm run check:spec-links`, `npm run check:spec-status` and\n179-`node scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.mjs --check origin/main` all gate CI, and\n180-`re-lint/require-status-matches-coverage` derives each `Status` row from its\n181-spec's citations. `re-lint/require-spec-link` gates in `eslint.config.mjs`: every test cites a\n182-statement, so an uncited new test fails the build. Its statement-side mirror,\n183-`require-statement-links`, runs at `warn` from `eslint.config.backlog.mjs` and\n184-reports without blocking - the severities the rule pair is designed for.\n185-\n186-## Commit Conventions\n187-\n188-### Format\n189-Follow conventional commits:\n190-```\n191-<type>(<scope>): <subject>\n192-\n193-<body>\n194-\n195-<footer>\n196-```\n197-\n198-### Types\n199-- `feat` - New feature (provider, tool, config option)\n200-- `fix` - Bug fix\n201-- `refactor` - Code restructuring without behavior change\n202-- `test` - Test additions or modifications\n203-- `docs` - Documentation only\n204-- `chore` - Build, deps, config, tooling\n205-- `perf` - Performance improvement\n206-\n207-### Scope\n208-Optional but recommended. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"call_c4bf88a14a5b448e9290644c","type":"tool_result","content":"* loop-bench/37\n  main\n  remotes/origin/HEAD -> origin/main\n  remotes/origin/loop-bench/37\n  remotes/origin/main\n---\ncommit 35b64a9e5b2d6c18004d20b53af9b6f686ad7d59\nAuthor: Saad <31802724+saadahmed95@users.noreply.github.com>\nDate:   Mon Oct 19 21:34:55 2026 +0300\n\n    fix(tools): refuse a duplicate tool name in ToolRegistry (#171)\n    \n    register stored a tool with a plain Map.set, so a second tool under a taken\n    name silently replaced the first: unreachable through execute, gone from\n    getDefinitions() and the system prompt, and nothing logged.\n    \n    register now throws Error('Duplicate tool name: <name>') for a name already\n    registered, checked against the name the definition resolves to at\n    registration, before anything is stored, so the first tool and its compiled\n    schema stay as they were.\n    \n    Behaviour change: code that re-registered a name now throws at startup; the\n    migration is to give the tools distinct names. No deprecation window: the\n    old behaviour was undocumented, silently lost a tool, and has no known user.\n    Ships in a minor release.\n    \n    Closes #55\n    \n    Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>\n\n CHANGELOG.md                                 |  4 ++-\n docs/adding-a-tool.md                        |  2 ++\n specs/hal-engine-duplicate-tool-name/spec.md | 21 ++++++++++++++++\n src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts     | 37 ++++++++++++++++++++++++++++\n src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts          |  2 ++\n 5 files changed, 65 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-)","is_error":false}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"491085a4-d2ca-4f17-85a3-818e99168ec0","uuid":"652360d1-eaf8-40e2-a818-b83d02217d72","timestamp":"2026-10-30T19:34:03.230Z","tool_use_result":{"stdout":"* loop-bench/37\n  main\n  remotes/origin/HEAD -> origin/main\n  remotes/origin/loop-bench/37\n  remotes/origin/main\n---\ncommit 35b64a9e5b2d6c18004d20b53af9b6f686ad7d59\nAuthor: Saad <31802724+saadahmed95@users.noreply.github.com>\nDate:   Mon Oct 19 21:34:55 2026 +0300\n\n    fix(tools): refuse a duplicate tool name in ToolRegistry (#171)\n    \n    register stored a tool with a plain Map.set, so a second tool under a taken\n    name silently replaced the first: unreachable through execute, gone from\n    getDefinitions() and the system prompt, and nothing logged.\n    \n    register now throws Error('Duplicate tool name: <name>') for a name already\n    registered, checked against the name the definition resolves to at\n    registration, before anything is stored, so the first tool and its compiled\n    schema stay as they were.\n    \n    Behaviour change: code that re-registered a name now throws at startup; the\n    migration is to give the tools distinct names. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"tool_result","content":"Exit code 1\n# A Duplicate Tool Name\n\n| Field  | Value                |\n| ------ | -------------------- |\n| Issue  | re-cinq/HALEngine#55 |\n| Status | Implemented          |\n\n`ToolRegistry.register` stored each tool under its name with a plain `Map.set`, so a second tool registered under a name already taken silently replaced the first. The first tool became unreachable through `execute` and vanished from `getDefinitions()` and the system prompt, and nothing logged the collision. A copy-pasted `name` in boot code is exactly the mistake a compiler cannot catch, and the model then answers with the wrong tool's data or none.\n\n## The contract\n\n- `register` refuses a name already registered: the second call throws `Error('Duplicate tool name: <name>')`, and the registry keeps the first tool, its definition and its executor ([validated by: throws Duplicate tool name: get_weather on the second register and keeps the first tool and its executor](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L320)).\n- The name checked is the one the definition resolves to at registration, for a plain definition and a definition function alike ([validated by: throws for a definition function that resolves to get_weather once a plain definition holds that name](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L341)).\n\n## Rationale\n\nRegistration runs in a consumer's boot code, so a collision becomes a startup failure naming the tool, the cheapest place to learn of it, instead of a silent loss at runtime.\n\n- **No last-wins mode, and no `unregister`.** Replacing a tool at runtime raises its own questions, such as calls already in flight and the tool list already sent to the model. Until an API answers them, a collision is always an error.\n- **No deprecation window.** The removed behaviour was undocumented, silently lost a tool, and has no known user: every in-tree caller registers distinct names. 1 });\n    }\n    return coverage;\n}\n/** Testable, unlinked statements — the `require-statement-links` view. */\nexport function unlinkedTestableStatements(content) {\n    return statementCoverage(content).unlinked;\n}\nexport function coverageTier(testable, linked) {\n    if (testable === 0) {\n        return \"vacuous\";\n    }\n    if (linked === 0) {\n        return \"none\";\n    }\n    return linked < testable ? {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"call_6248374c209b4db681c34428","type":"tool_result","content":"commit 50c2b45b9d07c4a34516d1c5d3f4916c0f893e4a\nAuthor: Lore Agent <lore-agent@re-cinq.com>\nDate:   Thu Sep 17 13:57:03 2026 +0000\n\n    test(orchestrator): pin config-installed hooks seam\n    \n    Add three config-level characterization tests through createHalEngine\n    and a new spec (specs/hal-engine-config-hooks) that cites them: an\n    engine with no orchestrator key still processes a message, a\n    config-installed beforeModelResponse hook receives the built base\n    prompt, and the clean-session hook order. Records the seam's three\n    measured semantics against chatOrchestrator.ts source lines.\n    \n    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>\n\n .lore/dod.md                          | 65 +++++++++++++++++++++++++++++\n specs/hal-engine-config-hooks/spec.md | 23 +++++++++++\n src/config.test.ts                    | 78 +++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++\n 3 files changed, 166 insertions(+)\n---\n# Config-Installed Orchestrator Hooks\n\n| Field  | Value                |\n| ------ | -------------------- |\n| Issue  | re-cinq/HALEngine#36 |\n| Status | In Progress          |\n\n`OrchestratorHooks` is the engine's only lifecycle seam, and `HalEngineConfig.orchestrator.hooks` is the supported way to install it: `createHalEngine` forwards the set to `createChatOrchestrator`, so a hook a deployer passes through the factory reaches the running orchestrator rather than sitting unread on the config object. This spec pins that forwarding and the measured semantics the seam already carries, so the hook-based features that follow in this epic — transparency disclosure, audit and usage recording, human oversight, provider failover — specify against real behaviour rather than against what the hook names suggest.\n\n## Installing hooks through config\n\n- A hook passed through `orchestrator.hooks` is forwarded to the orchestrator and fires ([validated by: forwards an orchestrator hook, so one passed through the config actually fires](../../src/config.test.ts#L17)).\n- An engine built with no `orchestrator` key at all still processes a message, so the field is optional in fact and not only in the type ([validated by: processes a message when the config declares no orchestrator key at all](../../src/config.test.ts#L93)).\n- A `beforeModelResponse` hook installed through config is handed the base system prompt built from `prompt`, which proves the hook reaches the orchestrator and is wired into the prompt pipeline rather than only being stored on the config ([validated by: hands a config-installed beforeModelResponse hook the built base system prompt, not merely storing it](../../src/config.test.ts#L106)). That the value the hook returns then replaces the system prompt the provider receives is exercised at the orchestrator layer, because `HalEngineConfig.provider` takes a `ProviderConfig` and offers no seam to inject a recording provider ([validated by: replaces system prompt with returned value](../../src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.test.ts#L194)).\n- For a session that completes without error the hooks fire in the order `beforeSession` → `beforeUserInput` → `afterUserInput` → `beforeModelResponse` → `afterModelResponse` → `afterSession` ([validated by: fires the lifecycle hooks in documented order for a session that completes without error](../../src/config.test.ts#L130)).\n\n## Measured semantics, unchanged by this issue\n\nThese three properties of `src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.ts` are recorded so the hook features that follow specify against real behaviour. This issue changes none of them; each is a separate, out-of-scope change owned by no issue in this epic.\n\n- `beforeSession` is awaited before the `try` block opens ([chatOrchestrator.ts#L74](../../src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.ts#L74)), so a throw there escapes before the `catch`/`finally` exist and skips both `onError` and `afterSession`.\n- The `catch` gates `onError` on `error instanceof Error` ([chatOrchestrator.ts#L127](../../src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.ts#L127)), so a rejection that is not an `Error` — a thrown string or object — bypasses `onError` entirely while still propagating to the caller.\n- `afterModelResponse` is called once per user message after the round loop exits ([chatOrchestrator.ts#L125](../../src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.ts#L125)), and is passed the `lastUsage` local — the most recent round's usage, not a sum across tool rounds.","is_error":false}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"491085a4-d2ca-4f17-85a3-818e99168ec0","uuid":"9463fe4a-ecff-46bc-92c6-3210d48cb802","timestamp":"2026-10-30T19:35:20.988Z","tool_use_result":{"stdout":"commit 50c2b45b9d07c4a34516d1c5d3f4916c0f893e4a\nAuthor: Lore Agent <lore-agent@re-cinq.com>\nDate:   Thu Sep 17 13:57:03 2026 +0000\n\n    test(orchestrator): pin config-installed hooks seam\n    \n    Add three config-level characterization tests through createHalEngine\n    and a new spec (specs/hal-engine-config-hooks) that cites them: an\n    engine with no orchestrator key still processes a message, a\n    config-installed beforeModelResponse hook receives the built base\n    prompt, and the clean-session hook order. This spec pins that forwarding and the measured semantics the seam already carries, so the hook-based features that follow in this epic — transparency disclosure, audit and usage recording, human oversight, provider failover — specify against real behaviour rather than against what the hook names suggest.\n\n## Installing hooks through config\n\n- A hook passed through `orchestrator.hooks` is forwarded to the orchestrator and fires ([validated by: forwards an orchestrator hook, so one passed through the config actually fires](../../src/config.test.ts#L17)).\n- An engine built with no `orchestrator` key at all still processes a message, so the field is optional in fact and not only in the type ([validated by: processes a message when the config declares no orchestrator key at all](../../src/config.test.ts#L93)).\n- A `beforeModelResponse` hook installed through config is handed the base system prompt built from `prompt`, which proves the hook reaches the orchestrator and is wired into the prompt pipeline rather than only being stored on the config ([validated by: hands a config-installed beforeModelResponse hook the built base system prompt, not merely storing it](../../src/config.test.ts#L106)). That the value the hook returns then replaces the system prompt the provider receives is exercised at the orchestrator layer, because `HalEngineConfig.provider` takes a `ProviderConfig` and offers no seam to inject a recording provider ([validated by: replaces system prompt with returned value](../../src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.test.ts#L194)).\n- For a session that completes without error the hooks fire in the order `beforeSession` → `beforeUserInput` → `afterUserInput` → `beforeModelResponse` → `afterModelResponse` → `afterSession` ([validated by: fires the lifecycle hooks in documented order for a session that completes without error](../../src/config.test.ts#L130)).\n\n## Measured semantics, unchanged by this issue\n\nThese three properties of `src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.ts` are recorded so the hook features that follow specify against real behaviour. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"call_39c925ac0c7f439a9d39ccdb","type":"tool_result","content":"/**\n * max-expects — one assertion per test. A test that checks five fields with\n * five `expect` calls stops at the first failure and hides the other four;\n * `expect(result).toEqual({...})` shows the whole diff at once, and a test\n * that genuinely needs two unrelated assertions is two tests.\n *\n * What counts: inside the callback of `it(...)` / `test(...)` and their\n * `.only` / `.skip` / `.each(...)` forms, every `expect(...)` call — the\n * ROOT call, so `expect(x).resolves.toEqual(y)` is one, not three.\n * `expect.assertions(n)` and `expect.hasAssertions()` are bookkeeping, not\n * assertions, and are not counted. Helper functions declared inside the test\n * body count toward the test that contains them: hiding assertions in a local\n * closure does not make the test smaller.\n *\n * Reported at the test call. Detect-only: which assertions merge into one\n * object and which become their own test is the author's call.\n */\nconst TEST_ROOTS = new Set([\"it\", \"test\"]);\nconst TEST_MODIFIERS = new Set([\"only\", \"skip\", \"each\", \"concurrent\"]);\nfunction isTestRoot(node) {\n    return node.type === \"Identifier\" && TEST_ROOTS.has(node.name);\n}\nfunction isTestModifier(node) {\n    return (node.type === \"MemberExpression\" &&\n        !node.computed &&\n        isTestRoot(node.object) &&\n        TEST_MODIFIERS.has(node.property.name));\n}\nfunction isTestCall(node) {\n    const { callee } = node;\n    if (isTestRoot(callee) || isTestModifier(callee)) {\n        return true;\n    }\n    // it.each(table)(\"name\", fn) — the callee is itself the `it.each(...)` call\n    return callee.type === \"CallExpression\" && isTestModifier(callee.callee);\n}\nfunction isExpectRootCall(node) {\n    return node.callee.type === \"Identifier\" && node.callee.name === \"expect\";\n}\nexport default {\n    meta: {\n        type: \"suggestion\",\n        docs: {\n            description: \"Enforce a maximum number of expect calls per it/test callback (default 1)\",\n        },\n        schema: [\n            {\n                type: \"object\",\n                properties: {\n                    max: { type: \"integer\", minimum: 1 },\n                },\n                additionalProperties: false,\n            },\n        ],\n        messages: {\n            tooManyExpects: \"Test has {{count}} expect calls (max {{max}}); assert one object with toEqual/toMatchObject or split the test\",\n        },\n    },\n    create(context) {\n        const max = context.options[0]?.max ?? 1;","is_error":false}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"491085a4-d2ca-4f17-85a3-818e99168ec0","uuid":"08f4a118-82d3-43eb-8caa-73da7b4533bf","timestamp":"2026-10-30T19:37:01.016Z","tool_use_result":{"stdout":"/**\n * max-expects — one assertion per test. Detect-only: which assertions merge into one\n * object and which become their own test is the author's call.\n */\nconst TEST_ROOTS = new Set([\"it\", \"test\"]);\nconst TEST_MODIFIERS = new Set([\"only\", \"skip\", \"each\", \"concurrent\"]);\nfunction isTestRoot(node) {\n    return node.type === \"Identifier\" && TEST_ROOTS.has(node.name);\n}\nfunction isTestModifier(node) {\n    return (node.type === \"MemberExpression\" &&\n        !node.computed &&\n        isTestRoot(node.object) &&\n        TEST_MODIFIERS.has(node.property.name));\n}\nfunction isTestCall(node) {\n    const { callee } = node;\n    if (isTestRoot(callee) || isTestModifier(callee)) {\n        return true;\n    }\n    // it.each(table)(\"name\", fn) — the callee is itself the `it.each(...)` call\n    return callee.type === \"CallExpression\" && isTestModifier(callee.callee);\n}\nfunction isExpectRootCall(node) {\n    return node.callee.type === \"Identifier\" && node.callee.name === \"expect\";\n}\nexport default {\n    meta: {\n        type: \"suggestion\",\n        docs: {\n            description: \"Enforce a maximum number of expect calls per it/test callback (default 1)\",\n        },\n        schema: [\n            {\n                type: \"object\",\n                properties: {\n                    max: { type: \"integer\", minimum: 1 },\n                },\n                additionalProperties: false,\n            },\n        ],\n        messages: {\n            tooManyExpects: \"Test has {{count}} expect calls (max {{max}}); assert one object with toEqual/toMatchObject or split the test\",\n        },\n    },\n    create(context) {\n        const max = context.options[0]?.max ?? 1;","stderr":"","interrupted":false,"isImage":false,"noOutputExpected":false},"tool_result_meta":[{"id":"call_39c925ac0c7f439a9d39ccdb","permission_decision":{"decision":"accept","source":"config","reason_type":"mode"}}]}

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"call_a3f7d36cb5e64eeeb0797a3e","type":"tool_result","content":"name: CI\n\non:\n  pull_request:\n  push:\n    branches: [main]\n  # Manual runs: re-checking a branch against a moved main, or confirming a gate after\n  # changing one, without pushing an empty commit.\n  workflow_dispatch:\n  # An advisory published after a merge is invisible until someone opens a pull request, and this\n  # repository can go days without one. Monday 07:00 UTC; only `build-chain` answers it.\n  schedule:\n    - cron: '0 7 * * 1'\n\n# Every job here only reads the checkout; the repo default is write.\npermissions:\n  contents: read\n\n# A newer push to the same branch supersedes an in-flight run. main is exempt:\n# every commit there should have its own recorded result.\nconcurrency:\n  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}\n  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }}\n\njobs:\n  verify:\n    name: Verify\n    # The scheduled run exists for the dependency audit; re-running the suite on an unchanged\n    # tree every Monday would report nothing new.\n    if: github.event_name != 'schedule'\n    runs-on: ubuntu-latest\n    steps:\n      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1\n        with:\n          persist-credentials: false\n          # Full history, not for this job but for the spec anchor check below:\n          # it resolves cited content from\n          # origin/main, which a shallow clone cannot serve.\n          fetch-depth: 0\n\n      - uses: actions/setup-node@820762786026740c76f36085b0efc47a31fe5020 # v7.0.0\n        with:\n          node-version: '22'\n          cache: npm\n\n      # --ignore-scripts so `prepare` does not build on install: what a lifecycle script\n      # runs is out of this workflow's control, and the Build step below is where a broken\n      # compile should be reported. Type check catches it earlier still.\n      - name: Install\n        run: npm ci --ignore-scripts\n\n      # Every `npm run` step below is one link of the `verify` script in\n      # package.json, in the same order - scripts/verify-script.test.ts holds\n      # the two together - and kept as separate steps so a red run names the\n      # gate that failed rather than a single opaque command.\n      - name: Type check\n        run: npm run typecheck\n\n      # example/ is outside tsconfig.json's rootDir, so nothing checked the one\n      # file the README and the guide are written against.\n      - name: Type check the example\n        run: npm run typecheck:example\n\n      - name: Lint (--max-warnings 0)\n        run: npm run eslint\n\n      # Reports, never blocks. The one rule it runs is `warn`, so the step exits\n      # 0 on its own and carries no continue-on-error: a non-zero exit here now\n      # means the config itself broke, and that should fail. Its findings render\n      # as warning annotations rather than failures, which is what a report on a\n      # passing check should look like.\n      #\n      # require-statement-links counts spec statements with no test behind them.\n      # Most of what it reports needs a test written rather than a line changed,\n      # so the count is meant to be visible on every run and to fall over time.\n      # Its test-side mirror, require-spec-link, is satisfied and gates in the\n      # Lint step above. Never add a rule here to escape a red gate -\n      # eslint.config.backlog.mjs says what belongs.\n      - name: Spec traceability backlog (report)\n        run: npm run lint:backlog","is_error":false}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"491085a4-d2ca-4f17-85a3-818e99168ec0","uuid":"76db2fb0-afa8-44f1-b6c3-125f18e2ff02","timestamp":"2026-10-30T19:39:24.390Z","tool_use_result":{"stdout":"name: CI\n\non:\n  pull_request:\n  push:\n    branches: [main]\n  # Manual runs: re-checking a branch against a moved main, or confirming a gate after\n  # changing one, without pushing an empty commit.\n  workflow_dispatch:\n  # An advisory published after a merge is invisible until someone opens a pull request, and this\n  # repository can go days without one.
